We next investigate the coherence properties of our devices by exciting the mechanical resonator with a pulse and registering its free decay via electromechanical readout (see appendix F). In this measurement, the electromechanical readout rate is a function of the detuning between the mechanical and microwave resonances $\Gamma_{\mathrm{em}} = g^2\kappa /(\Delta^2 +(\kappa /2)^2)$ . Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Let M be an LLM parameterized by $\theta$ that takes a text sequence $X = (x_{1}, \cdots, x_{m}) \in \mathbb{X}$ as input
$$ X = (x_{1}, \cdots, x_{m}) \in \mathbb{X} $$

The inputs may be drawn from a labeled dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(X^{(1)}, Y^{(1)}), \cdots, (X^{(N)}, Y^{(N)})\}$
$$ \mathcal{D} = \{(X^{(1)}, Y^{(1)}), \cdots, (X^{(N)}, Y^{(N)})\} $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quantity: statistical outcome measure conditioned on group membership
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: statistical outcome measure $\mathbb{M}_{Y}(G)$ conditioned on group membership
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
of a statistical outcome measure $\mathbb{M}_{Y}(G)$ conditioned on group membership:
$$
\left| \mathbb {M} _ {Y} (G) - \mathbb {M} _ {Y} (G ^ {\prime}) \right| \leq \epsilon \tag {1}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quantity: input with all social group identifiers removed
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: Let $X_{\setminus A}$ represent an input with all social group identifiers removed.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Let $X_{\setminus A}$ represent an input with all social group identifiers removed.
$$ \mathcal{M}(X;\theta) = \mathcal{M}(X_{\setminus A};\theta) $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quantity: generated text output associated with group $G_i$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
$$ \hat{Y}_i = (\hat{y}_1, \cdots, \hat{y}_n) \in \hat{\mathbb{Y}} $$
$\hat{Y}_i = (\hat{y}_1, \cdots, \hat{y}_n) \in \hat{\mathbb{Y}}$ generated text output associated with group $G_i$

$$ f(A,W)=(mean_{a_1\in A_1}s(a_1,W_1,W_2)-mean_{a_2\in A_2}s(a_2,W_1,W_2))/std_{a\in A}s(a,W_1,W_2) $$
WEAT $f(A,W)=(mean_{a_1\in A_1}s(a_1,W_1,W_2)-mean_{a_2\in A_2}s(a_2,W_1,W_2))/std_{a\in A}s(a,W_1,W_2)$

$$ f(S_A,S_W)=\frac{\Sigma_{i=1}^N v_i WEAT(S_{A_i},S_{W_i})}{\Sigma_{i=1}^N v_i} $$
CEAT $f(S_A,S_W)=\frac{\Sigma_{i=1}^N v_i WEAT(S_{A_i},S_{W_i})}{\Sigma_{i=1}^N v_i}$

$$ f(S)=\sum_{s\in S}|\cos(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}_{\text{gender}})\cdot\alpha_s| $$
Sentence Bias Score $f(S)=\sum_{s\in S}|\cos(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}_{\text{gender}})\cdot\alpha_s|$
$g(S)=\Sigma_{u\in U}\log P(u|U_{\backslash u},M;\theta)$
$f(G)=\Sigma_{a\in A}\Sigma_{\hat{Y}\in\hat{\mathbb{Y}}}C(a,\hat{Y})$
$f(w)=\Sigma_{a\in A}\Sigma_{\hat{Y}\in\hat{\mathbb{Y}}}C(a,\hat{Y})\mathbb{I}(C(w,\hat{Y})>0)$
$$ f(\hat{\mathbb{Y}})=\max_{\hat{Y}\in\hat{\mathbb{Y}}}c(\hat{Y}) $$

stereotypical associations are measured by a test statistic:

$$
f (A _ {1}, A _ {2}, W _ {1}, W _ {2}) = \sum_ {a _ {1} \in A _ {1}} s (a _ {1}, W _ {1}, W _ {2}) - \sum_ {a _ {2} \in A _ {2}} s (a _ {2}, W _ {1}, W _ {2}), \tag {3}
$$

where $s$ is a similarity measure defined as:

$$
s (a, W _ {1}, W _ {2}) = \operatorname{mean} _ {w _ {1} \in W _ {1}} \cos (\mathbf {a}, \mathbf {w} _ {\mathbf {1}}) - \operatorname{mean} _ {w _ {2} \in W _ {2}} \cos (\mathbf {a}, \mathbf {w} _ {\mathbf {2}}) \tag {4}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\operatorname{WEAT} \left(A _ {1}, A _ {2}, W _ {1}, W _ {2}\right) = \frac {\operatorname{mean} _ {a _ {1} \in A _ {1}} s \left(a _ {1} , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right) - \operatorname{mean} _ {a _ {2} \in A _ {2}} s \left(a _ {2} , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right)}{\operatorname{std} _ {a \in A _ {1} \cup A _ {2}} s \left(a , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right)}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Bias is measured by the effect size, given by

$$
\operatorname{WEAT} \left(A _ {1}, A _ {2}, W _ {1}, W _ {2}\right) = \frac {\operatorname{mean} _ {a _ {1} \in A _ {1}} s \left(a _ {1} , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right) - \operatorname{mean} _ {a _ {2} \in A _ {2}} s \left(a _ {2} , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right)}{\operatorname{std} _ {a \in A _ {1} \cup A _ {2}} s \left(a , W _ {1} , W _ {2}\right)}, \tag {5}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\operatorname{CEAT} \left(S _ {A _ {1}}, S _ {A _ {2}}, S _ {W _ {1}}, S _ {W _ {2}}\right) = \frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} v _ {i} \operatorname{WEAT} \left(S _ {A _ {1 i}} , S _ {A _ {2 i}} , S _ {W _ {1 i}} , S _ {W _ {2 i}}\right)}{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} v _ {i}}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
The magnitude of bias is calculated with a random-effects model, and is given by:

$$
\operatorname{CEAT} \left(S _ {A _ {1}}, S _ {A _ {2}}, S _ {W _ {1}}, S _ {W _ {2}}\right) = \frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} v _ {i} \operatorname{WEAT} \left(S _ {A _ {1 i}} , S _ {A _ {2 i}} , S _ {W _ {1 i}} , S _ {W _ {2 i}}\right)}{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} v _ {i}}, \tag {6}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\text { Sentence   Bias } (S) = \sum_ {s \in S, s \notin A} | \cos (\mathbf {s}, \mathbf {v} _ {\text { gender }}) \cdot \alpha_ {s} |$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Given a sentence S and a list of gendered words A, the metric computes the cosine similarity between the embedding of each word s in the sentence S and a gender direction $v_{gender}$ in the embedding space. The gender direction is identified by the difference between the embeddings of feminine and masculine gendered words, reduced to a single dimension with principal component analysis (PCA). The sentence importance weighs each word-level bias by a semantic importance score $\alpha_{s}$ , given by the number of times the sentence encoder's max-pooling operation selects the representation at s's position t.

$$
\text { Sentence   Bias } (S) = \sum_ {s \in S, s \notin A} | \cos (\mathbf {s}, \mathbf {v} _ {\text { gender }}) \cdot \alpha_ {s} | \tag {7}
$$

Bias is measured by the difference between normalized probability scores for two binary and opposing social group words.

$$
\operatorname{LPBS} (S) = \log \frac {p _ {a _ {i}}}{p _ {\text { prior } _ {i}}} - \log \frac {p _ {a _ {j}}}{p _ {\text { prior } _ {j}}} \tag {8}
$$

This metric measures the variance of predicted tokens for fill-in-the-blank template prompts over corresponding protected attribute words $a$ for different social groups:

$$
\operatorname{CBS} (S) = \frac {1}{| W |} \sum_ {w \in W} \operatorname{Var} _ {a \in A} \log \frac {p _ {a}}{p _ {\text { prior }}} \tag {9}
$$

For a sentence S, PLL is given by:

$$
\operatorname{PLL} (S) = \sum_ {s \in S} \log P (s | S _ {\backslash s}; \theta) \tag {10}
$$

For a sentence S, the metric is given by:

$$
\operatorname{CPS} (S) = \sum_ {u \in U} \log P (u | U _ {\backslash u}, M; \theta) \tag {11}
$$

Association Test (CAT) (Nadeem, Bethke, and Reddy 2021), introduced with the StereoSet dataset, also compares sentences. Similar to pseudo-log-likelihood, each sentence is paired with a stereotype, "anti-stereotype," and meaningless option, which are either fill-in-the-blank tokens or continuation sentences. The stereotype sentence illustrates a stereotype about a social group, while the anti-stereotype sentence replaces the social group with an instantiation that violates the given stereotype; thus, anti-stereotype sentences do not necessarily reflect pertinent harms. In contrast to pseudolog-likelihood, CAT considers $P(M|U,\theta)$ , rather than $P(U|M,\theta)$ . This can be framed as:

$$
\mathrm{CAT} (S) = \frac {1}{| M |} \sum_ {m \in M} \log P (m | U; \theta) \tag {12}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\mathrm{iCAT} (\mathcal {S}) = l m s \cdot \frac {\min (s s , 1 0 0 - s s)}{5 0}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Idealized CAT (iCAT) Score can be calculated from the same stereotype, anti-stereotype, and meaningless sentence options. Given a language modeling score (lms) that calculates

the percentage of instances that the model prefers a meaningful sentence option over a meaningless one, as well as a stereotype score (ss) that calculates the percentage of instances that the model prefers a stereotype option over an anti-stereotype one, Nadeem, Bethke, and Reddy (2021) define an idealized language model to have a language modeling score equal to 100 (i.e., it always chooses a meaningful option) and a stereotype score of 50 (i.e., it chooses an equal number of stereotype and anti-stereotype options).

$$
\mathrm{iCAT} (\mathcal {S}) = l m s \cdot \frac {\min (s s , 1 0 0 - s s)}{5 0} \tag {13}
$$

All Unmasked Likelihood (AUL) (Kaneko and Bollegala 2022) extends the CrowS-Pair Score and CAT to consider multiple correct candidate predictions. While pseudo-log-likelihood and CAT consider a single correct answer for a masked test example, AUL provides an unmasked sentence to the model and predicts all tokens in the sentence. The unmasked input provides the model with all information to predict a token, which can improve the prediction accuracy of the model, and avoids selection bias in the choice of which words to mask.

$$
\operatorname{AUL} (S) = \frac {1}{| S |} \sum_ {s \in S} \log P (s | S; \theta) \tag {14}
$$

Kaneko and Bollegala (2022) also provides a variation dubbed AUL with Attention Weights (AULA) that considers attention weights to account for different token importances. With $\alpha_{i}$ as the attention associated with $s_{i}$ , AULA is given by:

$$
\mathrm{AULA} (S) = \frac {1}{| S |} \sum_ {s \in S} \alpha_ {i} \log P (s | S; \theta) \tag {15}
$$

For CPS, CAT, AUL, and AULA, and for stereotyping sentences $S_{1}$ and less- or anti-stereotyping sentences $S_{2}$ , the bias score can be computed as:

$$
\operatorname{bias} _ {f \in \{\text { CPS }, \text { CAT }, \text { AUL }, \text { AULA } \}} (S) = \mathbb {I} \left(f (S _ {1}) > f (S _ {2})\right) \tag {16}
$$

As one of the coarsest measures, Social Group Substitutions (SGS) requires the response from an LLM model be identical under demographic substitutions. For an invariance metric $\psi$ such as exact match (Rajpurkar et al. 2016), and predicted outputs $\hat{Y}_{i}$ from an original input and $\hat{Y}_{j}$ from a counterfactual input, then:

$$
\operatorname{SGS} (\hat {Y}) = \psi \left(\hat {Y} _ {i}, \hat {Y} _ {j}\right) \tag {17}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\text { Co - Occurrence   Bias   Score } (w) = \log \frac {P (w | A _ {i})}{P (w | A _ {j})}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
For a token w and two sets of attribute words $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}$ , the bias score for each word is given by:

$$
\text { Co - Occurrence   Bias   Score } (w) = \log \frac {P (w | A _ {i})}{P (w | A _ {j})} \tag {18}
$$

For each group $G_{i} \in \mathbb{G}$ with associated protected attribute words $A_{i}$ , the count $\mathrm{DR}(G_i)$ is

$$
\mathrm{DR} (G _ {i}) = \sum_ {a _ {i} \in A _ {i}} \sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} C (a _ {i}, \hat {Y}) \tag {19}
$$
The vector of counts $\mathrm{DR} = [\mathrm{DR}(G_{1}), \ldots, \mathrm{DR}(G_{m})]$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quantity: Stereotypical Associations count for word $w$ and group $i$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Stereotypical Associations (ST) (Liang et al. 2022) measures bias

associated with specific terms, defined as:

$$
\mathrm{ST} (w) _ {i} = \sum_ {a _ {i} \in A _ {i}} \sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} C (a _ {i}, \hat {Y}) \mathbb {I} (C (w, \hat {Y}) > 0) \tag {20}
$$
Similar to Demographic Representation, the vector of counts $\mathrm{ST} = [\mathrm{ST}(w)_{i}, \ldots, \mathrm{ST}(w)_{k}]$

Gehman et al. (2020) leverage Expected Maximum Toxicity (EMT) computed over 25 generations... For a toxicity detector $c : \hat{Y} \rightarrow [0, 1]$ :

$$
\operatorname{EMT} (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \max _ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} c (\hat {Y}) \tag {21}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: The empirical probability of generating at least one text with a toxicity score $\geq 0.5$ over the 25 generations.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote: With Toxicity Probability (TP), they measure the empirical probability of generating at least one text with a toxicity score $\geq 0.5$ over the 25 generations, which captures how frequently the LLM generates text that is toxic. ... $$ \mathrm{TP} (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = P \left(\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \mathbb {I} (c (\hat {Y}) \geq 0. 5) \geq 1\right) \tag {22} $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: The fraction of generations that are toxic.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote: Other works have used the Toxic Fraction (TF), defined as the fraction of generations that are toxic (Liang et al. 2022). ... $$ \operatorname{TF} (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} [ \mathbb {I} (c (\hat {Y}) \geq 0. 5) ] \tag {23} $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: Measures how consistently a model generates language, as measured by a toxicity or sentiment classifier, given some protected attribute. Lack of parity is measured by the absolute difference in expected scores for two protected attribute values.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote: Score Parity (Sicilia and Alikhani 2023) measures how consistently a model generates language, as measured by a toxicity or sentiment classifier, given some protected attribute. For some scoring function $c: \hat{Y} \times A \to [0,1]$ , lack of parity can be measured by: $$ \text { Score   Parity } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = | \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} [ c (\hat {Y} _ {i}, i) | A = i ] - \mathbb {E} [ c (\hat {Y} _ {j}, j) | A = j ] | \tag {24} $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: Compares the sentiment of two sentences, generated with counterfactual prompts with a protected attribute replaced, using the Wasserstein-1 distance between the sentiment distributions.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote: Counterfactual Sentiment Bias (Huang et al. 2020) similarly compares the sentiment of two sentences, generated with counterfactual prompts with a protected attribute replaced. This metric uses the Wasserstein-1 distance $\mathcal{W}_{1}(\cdot)$ between the sentiment distributions from some classifier $c : \hat{Y} \to [0, 1]$ : $$ \text { Counterfactual   Sentiment   Bias } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \mathcal {W} _ {1} \left(P (c (\hat {\mathbb {Y}} _ {i}) | A = i), P (c (\hat {\mathbb {Y}} _ {j} | A = j)\right) \tag {25} $$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: Bias calculated as the variance across all generations for each style class, summed over all classes.
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote: Full Gen Bias (Smith et al. 2022) uses a style classifier to compute a style vector for each generated sentence $\hat{Y}_w$ corresponding to a term $w \in W$ in the prompt. Each element is the probability of a sentence belonging to one of $C$ style class, namely, $\left[c(\hat{Y})[1], \cdots, c(\hat{Y})[C]\right]$ . Bias is calculated as the variance across all generations: $$ \text { Full   Gen   Bias } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {C} \operatorname{Var} _ {w \in W} \left(\frac {1}{| \hat {\mathbb {Y}} _ {w} |} \sum_ {\hat {Y} _ {w} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}} _ {w}} c (\hat {Y} _ {w}) [ i ]\right) \tag {26} $$

HONEST (Nozza, Bianchi, and Hovy 2021) measures the number of hurtful completions. For identity-related template prompts and the top-k completions $\hat{Y}_{k}$ , the metric calculates how many completions contain words in the HurtLex lexicon (Bassignana et al. 2018), given by:

$$
\operatorname{HONEST} (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \frac {\sum_ {\hat {Y} _ {k} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}} _ {k}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y} _ {k}} \mathbb {I} _ {\text { HurtLex }} (\hat {y})}{| \hat {\mathbb {Y}} | \cdot k} \tag {27}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\text { Psycholinguistic   Norms } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \frac {\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} \operatorname{sign} (\text { affect - score } (\hat {y})) \text { affect - score } (\hat {y}) ^ {2}}{\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} | \text { affect - score } (\hat {y}) |}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
To measure the text-level norms, this metric takes the

weighted average of all psycholinguistic values:

$$
\text { Psycholinguistic   Norms } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \frac {\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} \operatorname{sign} (\text { affect - score } (\hat {y})) \text { affect - score } (\hat {y}) ^ {2}}{\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} | \text { affect - score } (\hat {y}) |} \tag {28}
$$

Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.definition: $\text { Gender   Polarity } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \frac {\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} \operatorname{sign} (\text { bias - score } (\hat {y})) \text { bias - score } (y) ^ {2}}{\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} | \text { bias - score } (\hat {y}) |}$
Bias_and_Fairness_in_Large_Language_Mode.quote:
Similar to psycholinguistic norms, the bias score is calculated as a weighted average of bias scores for all words in the text:

$$
\text { Gender   Polarity } (\hat {\mathbb {Y}}) = \frac {\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} \operatorname{sign} (\text { bias - score } (\hat {y})) \text { bias - score } (y) ^ {2}}{\sum_ {\hat {Y} \in \hat {\mathbb {Y}}} \sum_ {\hat {y} \in \hat {Y}} | \text { bias - score } (\hat {y}) |} \tag {29}

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.definition: The non-Hermitian Hamiltonian describing the optical interaction between two resonances coupled to the same radiation channel, given by the matrix expression in Eq. (1).
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote:
the optical interaction between them is described by the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian without taking into account the nonradiative damping terms [8, 13]:

$$
\begin{array}{l} H = \left( \begin{array}{c c} E _ {1} & k \\ k & E _ {2} \end{array} \right) - \mathrm {i} \left( \begin{array}{c c} \gamma_ {1} & \mathrm {e} ^ {\mathrm {i} \psi} \sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}} \\ \mathrm {e} ^ {\mathrm {i} \psi} \sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}} & \gamma_ {2} \end{array} \right) \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c} E _ {1} - \mathrm {i} \gamma_ {1} & k - \mathrm {i e} ^ {\mathrm {i} \psi} \sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}} \\ k - \mathrm {i e} ^ {\mat
hrm {i} \psi} \sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}} & E _ {2} - \mathrm {i} \gamma_ {2} \end{array} \right) \tag {1} \\ \end{array}
$$

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.definition: Represents the interference of radiating waves through far-field coupling.
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote: Therefore, parameter $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\psi}\sqrt{\gamma_1\gamma_2}$ represents the interference of radiating waves through far-field coupling [22].

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.definition: The eigenvalues of Hamiltonian (1), determined by the secular equation.
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote:
The eigenvalues of Hamiltonian (1) are determined by the secular equation and have the following form:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {E} = \frac {E _ {1} + E _ {2}}{2} - \mathrm {i} \frac {\gamma_ {1} - \gamma_ {2}}{2} \\ \pm \frac {1}{2} \sqrt {\left(\frac {E _ {1} - E _ {2}}{2} - \mathrm {i} \frac {\gamma_ {1} - \gamma_ {2}}{2}\right) ^ {2} + \left(k - \mathrm {i e} ^ {\mathrm {i} \psi} \sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}}\right) ^ {2}} \tag {2} \\ \end{array}
$$

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.definition: One of the two complex energy levels obtained using Friedrich-Wintgen condition (3); becomes purely real when condition (3) is satisfied, corresponding to a BIC.
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote:
Using Friedrich-Wintgen condition (3) we obtain the following expressions for two complex energy levels:

$$
\widetilde {E} _ {A} = \frac {E _ {1} + E _ {2}}{2} - p \frac {k}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}}} \frac {\gamma_ {1} + \gamma_ {2}}{2} \tag {4}
$$

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.definition: One of the two complex energy levels obtained using Friedrich-Wintgen condition (3); becomes more radiative when condition (3) is satisfied.
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote:
Using Friedrich-Wintgen condition (3) we obtain the following expressions for two complex energy levels:

$$
\widetilde {E} _ {B} = \frac {E _ {1} + E _ {2}}{2} + p \frac {k}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}}} \frac {\gamma_ {1} + \gamma_ {2}}{2} - \mathrm {i} (\gamma_ {1} + \gamma_ {2}) \tag {5}
$$

Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quantity: magnitude of the splitting of TE_{1,1,0} and TM_{1,1,1} branches
Bound_states_in_the_continuum_and_Fano_r.quote:
As follows from expressions (4) and (5), the magnitude of the splitting of $\mathrm{TE}_{1,1,0}$ and $\mathrm{TM}_{1,1,1}$ branches has the form:

$$
\Delta \sim \widetilde {E} _ {B} - \widetilde {E} _ {A} = 2 p \frac {k}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}}} \frac {\gamma_ {1} + \gamma_ {2}}{2} - \mathrm {i} \left(\gamma_ {1} + \gamma_ {2}\right) \tag {7}
$$

$$

$$

Distilling_the_Knowledge_in_a_Neural_Net.quote:
Neural networks typically produce class probabilities by using a “softmax” output layer that converts the logit, $z_{i}$ , computed for each class into a probability, $q_{i}$ , by comparing $z_{i}$ with the other logits.

$$
q _ {i} = \frac {\exp (z _ {i} / T)}{\sum_ {j} \exp (z _ {j} / T)} \tag {1}
$$

Distilling_the_Knowledge_in_a_Neural_Net.definition: \frac {\partial C}{\partial z _ {i}} = \frac {1}{T} \left(q _ {i} - p _ {i}\right) = \frac {1}{T} \left(\frac {e ^ {z _ {i} / T}}{\sum_ {j} e ^ {z _ {j} / T}} - \frac {e ^ {v _ {i} / T}}{\sum_ {j} e ^ {v _ {j} / T}}\right)
Distilling_the_Knowledge_in_a_Neural_Net.quote:
Each case in the transfer set contributes a cross-entropy gradient, $dC/dz_{i}$ , with respect to each logit, $z_{i}$ of the distilled model. If the cumbersome model has logits $v_{i}$ which produce soft target probabilities $p_{i}$ and the transfer training is done at a temperature of T, this gradient is given by:

$$
\frac {\partial C}{\partial z _ {i}} = \frac {1}{T} \left(q _ {i} - p _ {i}\right) = \frac {1}{T} \left(\frac {e ^ {z _ {i} / T}}{\sum_ {j} e ^ {z _ {j} / T}} - \frac {e ^ {v _ {i} / T}}{\sum_ {j} e ^ {v _ {j} / T}}\right) \tag {2}
$$

it is common to train the DNN to perform frame-by-frame classification by (locally) minimizing the cross entropy between the predictions made by the net and the labels given by a forced alignment with the ground truth sequence of states for each observation:

$$
\pmb {\theta} = \arg \max _ {\pmb {\theta} ^ {\prime}} P (h _ {t} | \mathbf {s} _ {t}; \pmb {\theta} ^ {\prime})
$$

where $\theta$ are the parameters of our acoustic model P

In this case, the forward propagating acoustic wave always experiences the same phase modulation when it traverses the electrodes and thus results in maximum modulation. On the other hand, the backward propagating wave effectively experiences a full $(2\pi)$ modulation cycle, which results in no net phase change. Formulation_for_scalable_optimization_of.definition: The quality factor $Q$ is a dimensionless lifetime, and $1 / Q$ is a dimensionless decay rate [14]. Mathematically, $Q$ is related to the frequency-domain Maxwell eigenvalue problem... The Q for the mode $\mathbf{E}^{n}(\mathbf{x})$ with eigen-frequency $\omega_{n}$ [14] is $Q = \frac {\mathrm{Re} [ \omega_ {n} ]}{- 2 \mathrm{Im} [ \omega_ {n} ]}.$
Formulation_for_scalable_optimization_of.quote:
There are two key figures of merit for a resonant mode $\mathbf{E}^n (\mathbf{x})$ of a cavity: quality factor $Q$ and modal volume $V$ . The quality factor $Q$ is a dimensionless lifetime, and $1 / Q$ is a dimensionless decay rate [14]. Mathematically, $Q$ is related to the frequency-domain Maxwell eigenvalue problem:

$$
\nabla \times \frac {1}{\mu (\mathbf {x})} \nabla \times \mathbf {E} ^ {n} (\mathbf {x}) = \omega_ {n} ^ {2} \varepsilon (\mathbf {x}) \mathbf {E} ^ {n} (\mathbf {x}) \tag {1}
$$

with radiation boundary conditions. Because of the lossy boundary conditions, the eigenproblem is non-Hermitian and the eigenvalues are complex. The Q for the mode $\mathbf{E}^{n}(\mathbf{x})$ with eigen-

frequency $\omega_{n}$ [14] is

$$
Q = \frac {\mathrm{Re} [ \omega_ {n} ]}{- 2 \mathrm{Im} [ \omega_ {n} ]}. \tag {2}
$$

Formulation_for_scalable_optimization_of.definition:
The modal volume V $[27]$ , defined as

$$
V = \frac {\int \varepsilon (\mathbf {x}) | \mathbf {E} ^ {n} (\mathbf {x}) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {x}}{\max \left\{\varepsilon (\mathbf {x}) | \mathbf {E} ^ {n} (\mathbf {x}) | ^ {2} \right\}}, \tag {3}
$$

is a measure of the volume within which the mode is confined.

For various values of L in experiments, we truncate the tokens to form the input sequence:

GHz_Rotation_of_an_Optically_Trapped_Nan.scope_ref: equation of motion of the particle's angular momentum
GHz_Rotation_of_an_Optically_Trapped_Nan.quote:
we consider the equation of motion of the particle's angular momentum $L$ , whose time rate of change equals the sum of all applied torques

$$
\frac {d}{d t} L = I \frac {d}{d t} \Omega_ {\mathrm{rot}} = \tau_ {\mathrm{opt}} + \tau_ {\mathrm{drag}}. \tag {1}
$$

method_ref.surface: equation of motion of the particle's angular momentum

GHz_Rotation_of_an_Optically_Trapped_Nan.quote: We consider three possible contributions to the optical torque $\tau_{\mathrm{opt}} = \tau_{\mathrm{abs}} + \tau_{\mathrm{brf}} + \tau_{\mathrm{shape}}$ .

The first component of the optical torque $\tau_{\mathrm{abs}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}\Delta s_{\mathrm{abs}}\mathcal{I}\lambda / (2\pi c)$ originates from absorbed photons that transfer their spin angular momentum to the particle [14].
The third optical torque component $\tau_{\mathrm{shape}} \propto \mathcal{I}$ describes the force arising due to a possible shape asymmetry of the particle [18].
In this regime, the viscous torque is given by $\tau_{\mathrm{drag}} = -I\Omega_{\mathrm{rot}} / t_{\mathrm{damp}}$ [26].

The damping time $t_{\mathrm{damp}} = \beta m\overline{v} / (p_{\mathrm{gas}}R^2)$ depends on the pressure $p_{\mathrm{gas}}$ , on the mean molecular velocity $\overline{v}$ , and on an accommodation factor $\beta$ that takes into account the efficiency with which molecules transfer angular momentum via collisions to the particle.

Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.definition: $$ w _ {P D G} (u, v) = \frac {w _ {A D G} (u , v) s (v)}{\sum_ {u ^ {\prime} \in V} w _ {A D G} (u ^ {\prime} , v) s (u ^ {\prime})} \tag {1} $$
Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quote:
That is, for directed edge $(u, v) \in E$ , the weight is

$$
w _ {P D G} (u, v) = \frac {w _ {A D G} (u , v) s (v)}{\sum_ {u ^ {\prime} \in V} w _ {A D G} (u ^ {\prime} , v) s (u ^ {\prime})} \tag {1}
$$

We compute the activation matrix in the $(l + 1)^{th}$ layer as $H^{(l+1)}$ , starting from $H^{0} = X$ .

To introduce the formulation, consider a simple form of layer-wise propagation:

$$
H ^ {(l + 1)} = \sigma \left(A H ^ {(l)} W ^ {(l)}\right) \tag {2}
$$
where $\sigma$ is an activation function such as $\operatorname{ReLU}(\cdot)=\max(0,\cdot)$ .

Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quantity: Hidden state of GRU sent at time step t
Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quote:
GRU $^{sent}$ recurrently updates hidden states at each time step t:

$$
\mathbf {h} _ {t} ^ {\text { sent }} = \mathrm{GRU} ^ {\text { sent }} (\mathbf {h} _ {t - 1} ^ {\text { sent }}, \mathbf {w} _ {t}) \tag {4}
$$

where $w_{t}$ is the word embedding for $w_{t}$ , $h_{t}^{sent}$ is the hidden state of GRU $^{sent}$ .

the input sentence embedding $x_{i}$ is the last hidden state:

$$
\mathbf {x} _ {i} = \mathbf {h} _ {L} ^ {\text { sent }} \tag {5}
$$

All sentence embeddings from the given document cluster are grouped as the node feature matrix X:

$$
X = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} - & \mathbf {x} _ {1} ^ {T} & - \\ - & \mathbf {x} _ {2} ^ {T} & - \\ & \vdots \\ - & \mathbf {x} _ {N} ^ {T} & - \end{array} \right] \tag {6}
$$

X is fed into GCN subsequently to obtain the final sentence embeddings $s_{i}$ that incorporate the graph representation of sentence relationships:

$$
Z = f (X, A) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} - & \mathbf {s} _ {1} ^ {T} & - \\ - & \mathbf {s} _ {2} ^ {T} & - \\ & \vdots \\ - & \mathbf {s} _ {N} ^ {T} & - \end{array} \right] \tag {7}
$$

Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quantity: Hidden state of GRU doc at time step t
Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.definition: $\mathbf {h} _ {t} ^ {d o c} = \mathrm{GRU} ^ {d o c} (\mathbf {h} _ {t - 1} ^ {d o c}, \mathbf {s} _ {t})$
Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quote:
GRU $^{doc}$ first builds the document embedding $d_{i}$ on top of sentence embeddings:

$$
\mathbf {h} _ {t} ^ {d o c} = \mathrm{GRU} ^ {d o c} (\mathbf {h} _ {t - 1} ^ {d o c}, \mathbf {s} _ {t}) \tag {8}
$$

$$ \mathbf {d} _ {i} = \mathbf {h} _ {| d _ {i} |} ^ {d o c} \tag {9} $$
In Eq 9, we extract the last hidden state as the document embedding for $d_{i}$ .

$$ \mathbf {C} = \frac {1}{M} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \mathbf {d} _ {i} \tag {10} $$
In Eq 10, we average over document embeddings to produce the cluster embedding C:

$$ f (s _ {i}) = \mathbf {v} ^ {T} \tanh (\mathbf {W} _ {1} \mathbf {C} + \mathbf {W} _ {2} \mathbf {s} _ {i}) \tag {11} $$
In Eq 11, we first calculate the score $f(s_{i})$ by considering the sentence embedding itself, $s_{i}$ , and the cluster embedding C for the global context of the multi-document.

$$ \operatorname{salience} (s _ {i}) = \frac {f (s _ {i})}{\sum_ {s _ {j} \in C} f (s _ {j})} \tag {12} $$
The score is then normalized as $\text{salience}(s_{i})$ via softmax in Eq 12.

$$ \mathcal {L} = - \sum_ {C} \sum_ {s _ {i} \in C} R (s _ {i}) \log (\text { salience } (s _ {i})) \tag {13} $$
The model is trained end-to-end to minimize the following cross-entropy loss between the salience prediction and the normalized ROUGE score of each sentence:

$$ R(s_{i}) = \text{softmax}(\alpha r(s_{i})) $$
$R(s_{i})$ is calculated by $R(s_{i}) = \text{softmax}(\alpha r(s_{i}))$ , where $r(s_{i})$ is the average of ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 Recall scores of sentence $s_{i}$ by measuring with the ground-truth human-written summaries.

Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.definition: constant rescaling factor to make the distribution sharper
Graph-based_Neural_Multi-Document_Summar.quote:
$$ R(s_{i}) = \text{softmax}(\alpha r(s_{i})) $$
$\alpha$ is a constant rescaling factor to make the distribution sharper.

GW170817_Observation_of_Gravitational_Wa.definition: The oscillation field decomposed into normal modes with factorized time and space dependence
GW170817_Observation_of_Gravitational_Wa.scope_ref: Damped harmonic oscillator model for tidally excited NS oscillation
GW170817_Observation_of_Gravitational_Wa.quote:
The NS oscillation vectors $\vec{\zeta}(t,\vec{r})$ satisfy an equation of the type see Kosovichev & Novikov (1992)

$$
\left(\rho \frac {d ^ {2}}{d t ^ {2}} + \mathcal {L}\right) \vec {\zeta} (t, \vec {r}) = - \rho \vec {\nabla} U (\vec {r}), \tag {11},
$$

where L is an operator characterizing the internal restoring force of the star. In order to apply this toy model of a damped harmonic oscillator to the tidally excited NS oscillation, we decompose the oscillation field $\vec{\zeta}(t,\vec{r})$ into normal modes with factorized time and space dependence:

$$
\vec {\zeta} (t, \vec {r}) = \sum_ {n, \ell , m} q _ {n \ell m} (t) \vec {\xi} _ {n \ell m} (\vec {r}), \tag {12},
$$

method_ref.surface: Damped harmonic oscillator model for tidally excited NS oscillation

Knowledge_Inheritance_for_Pre-trained_La.quantity: Corpora for training the larger PLM
Knowledge_Inheritance_for_Pre-trained_La.quote:
our goal is leveraging $\mathcal{M}_{S}$ 's knowledge to efficiently train a larger PLM $\mathcal{M}_{L}$ on the corpora $\mathcal{D}_{L} = \{(\mathbf{x}_{i}, \mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{D}_{L}\right|}$ .
$$ \mathcal{D}_{L} = \{(\mathbf{x}_{i}, \mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{D}_{L}\right|} $$

imparting $M_{S}$ 's knowledge to $M_{L}$ on $D_{L}$ is implemented by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between two probability distributions output by $M_{S}$ and $M_{L}$ on the same input $x_{i} \in D_{L}$ , i.e., $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KI}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \mathcal{M}_{S}) = \tau^{2}\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{S}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \tau) || \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{L}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \tau))$ .
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KI}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \mathcal{M}_{S}) = \tau^{2}\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{S}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \tau) || \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{L}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}; \tau)) $$

Both $L_{SELF}$ and $L_{KI}$ are balanced with an inheritance rate $\alpha$ :
$$ \begin{array}{l} \mathcal {L} (\mathcal {D} _ {L}; \mathcal {M} _ {S}) = \sum_ {(\mathbf {x} _ {i}, \mathbf {y} _ {i}) \in \mathcal {D} _ {L}} (1 - \alpha) \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm{SELF}} (\mathbf {x} _ {i}, \mathbf {y} _ {i}) + \alpha \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm{KI}} (\mathbf {x} _ {i}; \mathcal {M} _ {S}) \\ = \sum_ {(\mathbf {x} _ {i}, \mathbf {y} _ {i}) \in \mathcal {D} _ {L}} (1 - \alpha) \mathcal {H} (\mathbf {y} _ {i}, \mathcal {P} _ {\mathcal {M} _ {L}} (\mathbf {x} _ {i}; 1)) \tag {1} \\ + \alpha \tau^ {2} \mathrm{KL} (\mathcal {P} _ {\mathcal {M} _ {S}} (\mathbf {x} _ {i}; \tau) | | \mathcal {P} _ {\mathcal {M} _ {L}} (\mathbf {x} _ {i}; \tau))). \\ \end{array} $$

Specifically, for a total training steps of T, we linearly decay $\alpha_{t}$ with a slope of $\frac{\alpha_{T}}{T}$ . The student only inherits knowledge from the teacher for $\frac{T}{\alpha_{T}}$ steps, and then conducts pure self-learning, i.e., $\alpha_{t} = \max(1 - \alpha_{T} \times \frac{t}{T}, 0)$ .

$$ \alpha_{t} = \max(1 - \alpha_{T} \times \frac{t}{T}, 0) $$

Laser_cooling_of_a_nanomechanical_oscill.quantity: time average detected power spectral density on the photoreceiver
Laser_cooling_of_a_nanomechanical_oscill.definition: $P | _ {\omega_ {s}} = \frac {a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}}{8 R _ {L}} | r (\omega_ {s}) | ^ {2} \left[ 3 + 4 \cos (\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}} t - \varphi) + \frac {1}{2} \cos (2 \omega_ {\mathrm{LI}} t - 2 \varphi) + \mathcal {O} (2 \omega_ {\mathrm{l}}) \right]$
Laser_cooling_of_a_nanomechanical_oscill.quote:
We can now write the time average detected power spectral density on the photoreceiver (D1 in Figure (5)) by taking the absolute square value of the reflected field and keeping only the terms with frequency smaller than the detector bandwidth. In this case:

$$
P | _ {\omega_ {s}} = \frac {a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}}{8 R _ {L}} | r (\omega_ {s}) | ^ {2} \left[ 3 + 4 \cos (\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}} t - \varphi) + \frac {1}{2} \cos (2 \omega_ {\mathrm{LI}} t - 2 \varphi) + \mathcal {O} (2 \omega_ {\mathrm{l}}) \right].
$$

This signal is then sent to the lock-in which can measure independently the in-phase (X) and quadrature (Y) power spectral densities at $\omega_{LI}$ :

$$
X | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} = \frac {a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}}{4 R _ {L}} | r (\omega_ {s}) | ^ {2} \cos (\varphi)
$$

This signal is then sent to the lock-in which can measure independently the in-phase (X) and quadrature (Y) power spectral densities at $\omega_{LI}$ :

$$
X | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} = \frac {a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}}{4 R _ {L}} | r (\omega_ {s}) | ^ {2} \cos (\varphi)
$$

$$
Y | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} = \frac {a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}}{4 R _ {L}} | r (\omega_ {s}) | ^ {2} \sin (\varphi) \tag {F4}
$$

It is then easy to see the reflection amplitude and phase are given by

$$
\left| r \left(\omega_ {s}\right) \right| ^ {2} = \frac {4 R _ {L}}{a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}} \sqrt {X \left| _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} ^ {2} + Y \right| _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} ^ {2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \tan (\varphi) = \frac {Y | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}}}{X | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}}}.
$$

It is then easy to see the reflection amplitude and phase are given by

$$
\left| r \left(\omega_ {s}\right) \right| ^ {2} = \frac {4 R _ {L}}{a _ {o} ^ {2} \beta^ {2} R _ {\mathrm{PD}} G _ {\mathrm{PD}}} \sqrt {X \left| _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} ^ {2} + Y \right| _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}} ^ {2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \tan (\varphi) = \frac {Y | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}}}{X | _ {\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}}}.
$$

From the imparted change in the phase the signal delay is then calculated as:

$$
\tau^ {\mathrm{(R)}} = \frac {\varphi}{\omega_ {\mathrm{LI}}}
$$

We then perform a least squares fit to a Lorentzian function of the form

$$
L (\omega) = \frac {A}{\left(\frac {\omega - \omega_ {m}}{2 \gamma}\right) ^ {2} + 1} \tag {G1}
$$

The spectral power is then given simply by

$$
P _ {\omega_ {m}} = \frac {A \gamma}{4}. \tag {G2}
$$

$$

Laser_cooling_of_a_nanomechanical_oscill.quantity: Cumulative error for the number of measured phonons
Laser_cooling_of_a_nanomechanical_oscill.quote:
We can calculate the cumulative error for the number of measured phonons on the cavity using this equation and based upon on the measurable variables which gives:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\Delta \bar {n}}{\bar {n}} = \left[ \frac {\delta \omega_ {0} ^ {2}}{\omega_ {0} ^ {2}} + \frac {\delta \kappa_ {e} ^ {2}}{\kappa_ {e} ^ {2}} + \frac {\delta P _ {\text {in}} ^ {2}}{P _ {\text {in}} ^ {2}} + \frac {\delta P _ {\mathrm{RSA}} ^ {2}}{P _ {\mathrm{RSA}} ^ {2}} + \frac {\delta \gamma_ {i} ^ {2}}{(\gamma - \gamma_ {i}) ^ {2}} + \frac {\delta \gamma^ {2}}{\gamma - \gamma_ {i}) ^ {2}} + \dots \right. \tag {H4} \\ \left. + \left(\frac {\kappa / 2}{(\kappa / 2) ^ {2} + (\Delta - \omega_ {m}) ^ {2}} - \frac {1}{\kappa}\right) ^ {2} \delta \kappa^ {2} + \left(\frac {2 (\Delta - \omega_ {m})}{(\kappa / 2) ^ {2} + (\Delta - \omega_ {m}) ^ {2}}\right) ^ {2} \delta \Delta^ {2} + \left(\frac {2 (\Delta - \omega_ {m})}{(\kappa / 2) ^ {2} + (\Delta - \omega_ {m}) ^ {2}}\right) ^ {2} \delta \omega_ {m} ^ {2} \right] ^ {1 / 2} \\ \end{array}
$$

The starting point of the analysis is the cavity-perturbation formula for dielectric cavities [33],

$$
\frac {\omega - \omega_ {0}}{\omega_ {0}} \approx - \frac {1}{2} \frac {\int \delta \varepsilon (\mathbf {r}) | \mathbf {E} (\mathbf {r}) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {r}}{\int \varepsilon (\mathbf {r}) | \mathbf {E} (\mathbf {r}) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {r}}. \tag {I1}
$$

Length-Controlled_AlpacaEval_A_Simple_Wa.quantity: Logistic regression model predicting preference y=1
Length-Controlled_AlpacaEval_A_Simple_Wa.definition: $q_{\theta, \phi, \psi}(y = 1 | z_{m}, z_{b}, m, b, x) := \text{logistic}\left(\theta_{m} - \theta_{b} + \phi_{m, b} \cdot \tanh\left(\frac{\operatorname{len}(z_{m}) - \operatorname{len}(z_{b})}{\operatorname{std}(\operatorname{len}(z_{m}) - \operatorname{len}(z_{b}))}\right) + (\psi_{m} - \psi_{b}) \gamma_{x}\right)$
Length-Controlled_AlpacaEval_A_Simple_Wa.quote:
we will model the AlpacaEval predictions $f(z_{m}, z_{b}, x)$ with a logistic regression that has 3 terms: model, length, and instruction.

$$
\begin{array}{l} q _ {\theta , \phi , \psi} (y = 1 | z _ {m}, z _ {b}, m, b, x) := \\
\text { logistic } \left(\underbrace {\theta_ {m} - \theta_ {b}} _ {\text { Model }} + \underbrace {\phi_ {m , b} \cdot \tanh \left(\frac {\operatorname{len} (z _ {m}) - \operatorname{len} (z _ {b})}{\operatorname{std} (\operatorname{len} (z _ {m}) - \operatorname{len} (z _ {b}))}\right)} _ {\text { Length }} + \underbrace {(\psi_ {m} - \psi_ {b}) \gamma_ {x}} _ {\text { Instruction }}\right). \tag {1} \\
\end{array}
$$

Length-Controlled_AlpacaEval_A_Simple_Wa.quote:
and symmetry property, i.e., $q(y \mid z_{m}, z_{b}, b, m, x) = 1.0 - q(y \mid z_{b}, z_{m}, b, m, x)$

$$ q(y \mid z_{m}, z_{b}, b, m, x) = 1.0 - q(y \mid z_{b}, z_{m}, b, m, x) $$

we obtain the length corrected win rate estimate as

Within a given model then, the likelihood $\Pr\left(\mathbf{d}|\boldsymbol{\theta},H\right)$ can be calculated for any values of the model parameters $\theta$ . However, as outlined above, cosmologists want statistical inferences, i.e., we want to learn more about our model and its parameters from the data, by calculating the posterior distribution $\Pr\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathbf{d},H\right)$ . This distribution contains all the information about the model supplied by the data, as well as all the information we had about the model other than that provided by the data: this can be seen by applying the product rule of conditional probability to give Bayes' theorem,

$$
\operatorname * {P r} (\boldsymbol {\theta} | \mathbf {d}, H) = \frac {\operatorname* {P r} (\mathbf {d} | \boldsymbol {\theta} , H) \operatorname* {P r} (\boldsymbol {\theta} | H)}{\operatorname* {P r} (\mathbf {d} | H)}. \tag {B.3}
$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: The percentage of words in the summary that are from the source article, measuring the extent to which a summary is derivative of a text.
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
Extractive fragment coverage is the percentage of words in the summary that are from the source article, measuring the extent to which a summary is derivative of a text:

$$
\text { COVERAGE } (A, S) = \frac {1}{| S |} \sum_ {f \in F (A, S)} | f | \tag {1}
$$

$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.symbol: $C O M P R E S S I O N (A, S)$

$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: An attention distribution calculated as in (Bahdanau et al., 2014) and is used to get the context vector $h_{t}^{*}$.
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
An attention distribution $a^{t}$ is calculated as in (Bahdanau et al., 2014) and is used to get the context vector $h_{t}^{*}$ , which is a weighted sum of the encoder hidden states, representing the semantic meaning of the related document content for this decoding time step:

$$
\begin{array}{l} e _ {i} ^ {t} = v ^ {T} \mathrm{tanh} (W _ {h} h _ {i} + W _ {s} d _ {t} + b _ {a t t n}) \\
a ^ {t} = \operatorname{softmax} \left(e ^ {t}\right) \tag {4} \\
\end{array}
$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: A weighted sum of the encoder hidden states, representing the semantic meaning of the related document content for this decoding time step.
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
An attention distribution $a^{t}$ is calculated as in (Bahdanau et al., 2014) and is used to get the context vector $h_{t}^{*}$ , which is a weighted sum of the encoder hidden states, representing the semantic meaning of the related document content for this decoding time step:

$$
\begin{array}{l} e _ {i} ^ {t} = v ^ {T} \mathrm{tanh} (W _ {h} h _ {i} + W _ {s} d _ {t} + b _ {a t t n}) \\
a ^ {t} = \operatorname{softmax} \left(e ^ {t}\right) \tag {4} \\
\end{array}
$$

$$
h _ {t} ^ {*} = \sum_ {i} a _ {i} ^ {t} h _ {i} ^ {t}
$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: The vocabulary distribution produced by passing the context vector $h_{t}^{*}$ and the decoder hidden state $d_{t}$ to two linear layers.
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
The context vector $h_{t}^{*}$ and the decoder hidden state $d_{t}$ are then passed to two linear layers to produce the vocabulary distribution $P_{vocab}$ .

$$
P _ {v o c a b} = \operatorname{softmax} (V ^ {\prime} (V [ d _ {t}, h _ {t} ^ {*} ] + b) + b ^ {\prime})
$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: It is the sum of the attention weights over all the word occurrences: $$ P _ {c o p y} = \sum_ {i: w _ {i} = w} a _ {i} ^ {t} \tag {5} $$
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
For each word, there is also a copy probability $P_{copy}$ . It is the sum

of the attention weights over all the word occurrences:

$$
P _ {c o p y} = \sum_ {i: w _ {i} = w} a _ {i} ^ {t} \tag {5}
$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition:
The pointer-generator network has a soft switch $p_{gen}$ , which indicates whether to generate a word from vocabulary by sampling from $P_{vocab}$ , or to copy a word from the source sequence by sampling from the copy probability $P_{copy}$ .

$$
p _ {g e n} = \sigma (w _ {h ^ {*}} ^ {T} h _ {t} ^ {*} + w _ {d} ^ {T} d _ {t} + w _ {x} ^ {T} x _ {t} + b _ {p t r}) \quad (6)
$$

$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition:
Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) is an approach for combining query-relevance with information-novelty in the context of summarization (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998). MMR produces a ranked list of the candidate sentences based on the relevance and redundancy to the query, which can be used to extract sentences. The score is calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{MMR} = \underset {D _ {i} \in R \backslash S} {\operatorname{argmax}} \left[ \lambda \operatorname{Sim} _ {1} \left(D _ {i}, Q\right) \right. \tag {8} \\ \left. - (1 - \lambda) \max _ {D _ {j} \in S} \operatorname{Sim} _ {2} \left(D _ {i}, D _ {j}\right) \right] \\ \end{array}
$$

$$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quantity: word-level sentence embeddings of the document
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: The word-level sentence embeddings of the document $h_{D}^{w} = [h_{s_{1}}^{w}, h_{s_{2}}^{w}, ..h_{s_{n}}^{w}]$ will be a sequence which is fed into a sentence-level LSTM network.
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote: The word-level sentence embeddings of the document $h_{D}^{w} = [h_{s_{1}}^{w}, h_{s_{2}}^{w}, ..h_{s_{n}}^{w}]$ will be a sequence which is fed into a sentence-level LSTM network.

We then get the final sentence-level embeddings $h_{D}^{s} = [h_{1}^{s}, h_{2}^{s}, ..h_{n}^{s}]$ (we omit the subscript for sentences s).
$$ h_{D}^{s} = [h_{1}^{s}, h_{2}^{s}, ..h_{n}^{s}] $$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quantity: MMR score for an input sentence i
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: $\mathrm{MMR} _ {i} = \lambda \operatorname{Sim} _ {1} \left(h _ {i} ^ {s}, s _ {\text { sum }}\right) - (1 - \lambda) \max _ {s _ {j} \in D, j \neq i} \operatorname{Sim} _ {2} \left(h _ {i} ^ {s}, h _ {j} ^ {s}\right)$
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
The MMR score for an input sentence i is then defined as:
$$ \begin{array}{l} \mathrm{MMR} _ {i} = \lambda \operatorname{Sim} _ {1} \left(h _ {i} ^ {s}, s _ {\text { sum }}\right) \\ - (1 - \lambda) \max _ {s _ {j} \in D, j \neq i} \operatorname{Sim} _ {2} \left(h _ {i} ^ {s}, h _ {j} ^ {s}\right) \tag {9} \\ \end{array} $$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quantity: similarity function between candidate sentence and summary sentence
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: $\mathrm{Sim} _ {1} = h _ {i} ^ {s T} W _ {\mathrm{Sim}} s _ {s u m}$
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
Now we define the similarity function between each candidate sentence $h_{i}^{s}$ and summary sentence $s_{sum}$ to be:
$$ \mathrm{Sim} _ {1} = h _ {i} ^ {s T} W _ {\mathrm{Sim}} s _ {s u m} \tag {11} $$

Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.definition: $v _ {i j} = \tanh \left(h _ {j} ^ {s T} W _ {s e l f} h _ {i} ^ {s}\right)$
Multi-News_a_Large-Scale_Multi-Document_.quote:
we choose to apply a self-attention model on $h_{i}^{s}$ and all the other candidates $h_{j}^{s} \in h_{D}^{s}$ . We then choose the largest weight as the final score:
$$ v _ {i j} = \tanh \left(h _ {j} ^ {s T} W _ {s e l f} h _ {i} ^ {s}\right) $$

MUSE_Machine_Unlearning_Six-Way_Evaluati.quote:
We want to preserve performance on a retain set $D_{retain} = D_{train} \setminus D_{forget}$ , and we also evaluate the model on an in-distribution but disjoint hold-out set $D_{holdout}$ which the model has never been trained on.
$$ D_{retain} = D_{train} \setminus D_{forget} $$

Ideally, an unlearned model should behave as if it had never seen the forget set, exhibiting similar behavior to a retrained model on any corpus D such that $m(f_{\text{unlearn}}, \mathcal{D}) \approx m(f_{\text{retrain}}, \mathcal{D})$ , where m represents any evaluation metric.
$$ m(f_{\text{unlearn}}, \mathcal{D}) \approx m(f_{\text{retrain}}, \mathcal{D}) $$

We quantify the verbatim memorization VerbMem by prompting the model with the first l tokens from a sequence $x_{[:l]} \in D_{forget}$ and comparing the continuation outputted by the model f to the true continuation $x_{[l+1:]} \in D_{forget}$ using the ROUGE-L F1 score (Lin, 2004).
$$
\operatorname{VerbMem} (f, \mathcal {D}) := \frac {1}{| \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} |} \sum_ {x \in \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }}} \operatorname{ROUGE} (f (x _ {[: l ]}), x _ {[ l + 1: ]})
$$

We then average the ROUGE scores for all question-answer pairs in $\mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}}$ to compute the knowledge memorization score KnowMem:
$$
\operatorname{KnowMem} (f, \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }}) := \frac {1}{| \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} |} \sum_ {(q, a) \in \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }}} \operatorname{ROUGE} (f (q), a)
$$

MUSE_Machine_Unlearning_Six-Way_Evaluati.definition: $\text { PrivLeak } := \frac {\text { AUC } (f _ {\text { unlearn }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }}) - \text { AUC } (f _ {\text { retrain }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }})}{\text { AUC } (f _ {\text { retrain }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }})}$
MUSE_Machine_Unlearning_Six-Way_Evaluati.quote:
By comparing the AUC score with that of the retrained model, we define $^{4}$
$$
\text { PrivLeak } := \frac {\text { AUC } (f _ {\text { unlearn }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }}) - \text { AUC } (f _ {\text { retrain }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }})}{\text { AUC } (f _ {\text { retrain }} ; \mathcal {D} _ {\text { forget }} , \mathcal {D} _ {\text { holdout }})},
$$

MUSE_Machine_Unlearning_Six-Way_Evaluati.definition: $p _ {f _ {\text {   unlearn   }}} (\cdot | x) = p _ {f _ {\text {   target   }}} (\cdot | x) - \alpha (p _ {f _ {\text {   reinforce   }}} (\cdot | x) - p _ {f _ {\text {   target   }}} (\cdot | x))$
MUSE_Machine_Unlearning_Six-Way_Evaluati.quote: $$ p _ {f _ {\text {   unlearn   }}} (\cdot | x) = p _ {f _ {\text {   target   }}} (\cdot | x) - \alpha (p _ {f _ {\text {   reinforce   }}} (\cdot | x) - p _ {f _ {\text {   target   }}} (\cdot | x)) $$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) = \mathbf {1} [ \hat {y} \text {i s c o r r e c t f o r} x ]$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Denote $x$ as the input, $\hat{y}$ as the model's output, estimated confidence as $s(x, \hat{y})$ , and $\mathcal{C}(x, \hat{y}) \in \{0, 1\}$ as the correctness function. Formally,

$$
\mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) = \mathbf {1} [ \hat {y} \text {i s c o r r e c t f o r} x ]. \tag {1}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (\mathbf {s})$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quantity: Brier score used in response calibration
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (\mathbf {s}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(s _ {i} - \mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y} _ {i}\right)\right) ^ {2}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Brier score used in response calibration is

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (\mathbf {s}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(s _ {i} - \mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y} _ {i}\right)\right) ^ {2}. \tag {3}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mu (x, f _ {\theta}) \triangleq \mathbb {P} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) = 1 ] = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) ]$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
For a given input $x$ , we define the model's expected accuracy as

$$
\mu (x, f _ {\theta}) \triangleq \mathbb {P} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) = 1 ] = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) ], \tag {4}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: The perfect calibration for capability calibration is defined as the expected accuracy $\mu(x, f_{\theta})$.
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
The perfect calibration for capability calibration is

$$
s ^ {*} = \mu (x, f _ {\theta}). \tag {6}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {c a p a b i l i t y}} (\mathbf {s})$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: The capability calibration Brier score is defined as the mean squared error between estimated confidences $s_i$ and expected accuracies $\mu_i$.
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Specifically, let $\mu_{i}$ be the expected accuracy $\mu (x_i,f_\theta)$ , the capability calibration Brier score is

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {c a p a b i l i t y}} (\mathbf {s}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(s _ {i} - \mu_ {i}\right) ^ {2}. \tag {7}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quantity: Optimal confidence estimator for response calibration
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: Minimizing the Brier score for response calibration yields the optimal confidence estimator $s _ {\mathrm {r e s p}} ^ {*} (x, \hat {y}) = \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y})$.
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Minimizing the Brier scores for response calibration (Equation (3)) and capability calibration (Equation (7)) yields distinct optimal confidence estimators:

$$
\begin{array}{l} s _ {\mathrm {r e s p}} ^ {*} (x, \hat {y}) = \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) \in \{0, 1 \}, \\
s _ {\mathrm {c a p}} ^ {*} (x, f _ {\theta}) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) ] \in [ 0, 1 ]. \tag {8} \\
\end{array}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quantity: Optimal confidence estimator for capability calibration
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: Minimizing the Brier score for capability calibration yields the optimal confidence estimator $s _ {\mathrm {c a p}} ^ {*} (x, f _ {\theta}) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) ]$.
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Minimizing the Brier scores for response calibration (Equation (3)) and capability calibration (Equation (7)) yields distinct optimal confidence estimators:

$$
\begin{array}{l} s _ {\mathrm {r e s p}} ^ {*} (x, \hat {y}) = \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) \in \{0, 1 \}, \\
s _ {\mathrm {c a p}} ^ {*} (x, f _ {\theta}) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x)} [ \mathcal {C} (x, \hat {y}) ] \in [ 0, 1 ]. \tag {8} \\
\end{array}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathbb {E} \big [ \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} \big ]$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: The expectation of response calibration loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Brier}}^{\mathrm{response}}$ on the model's output distribution is defined as the average over inputs of the expected squared error between confidence and correctness.
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Given a set of estimated confidence $\mathbf{s}$ , define the expectation of response calibration loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Brier}}^{\mathrm{response}}$ on the model's output distribution as

$$
\mathbb {E} \big [ \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} \big ] \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} \left[ (s _ {i} - \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y})) ^ {2} \right].
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {c a p a b i l i t y}}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {c a p a b i l i t y}} = \underbrace {\mathbb {E} [ \mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {r e s p o n s e}} ]} _ {\text {r e s p o n s e c a l i b r a t i o n}} - \underbrace {\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} V a r (\mathcal {C} (x _ {i} , \hat {y}))} _ {\text {o u t p u t c o r r e c t n e s s v a r i a n c e}}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Decoupling output correctness variance from response calibration, we get capability calibration:

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {c a p a b i l i t y}} = \underbrace {\mathbb {E} [ \mathcal {L} _ {\text {B r i e r}} ^ {\text {r e s p o n s e}} ]} _ {\text {r e s p o n s e c a l i b r a t i o n}} - \underbrace {\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} V a r (\mathcal {C} (x _ {i} , \hat {y}))} _ {\text {o u t p u t c o r r e c t n e s s v a r i a n c e}}, \tag {9}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $V a r \left(\mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y}\right)\right) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} \left[ \mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y}\right) ^ {2} \right] - \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} [ \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y}) ] ^ {2}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
where

$$
\begin{array}{l} V a r \left(\mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y}\right)\right) = \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} \left[ \mathcal {C} \left(x _ {i}, \hat {y}\right) ^ {2} \right] \tag {10} \\ - \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} [ \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y}) ] ^ {2}. \\ \end{array}
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\hat {\mu} = \frac {c}{k _ {\mathrm {e v a l}}}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
The estimated expected accuracy is:

$$
\hat {\mu} = \frac {c}{k _ {\mathrm {e v a l}}}.
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\hat{y}_i \sim f_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x_i)$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote: For each input $x_{i}$ , let $\hat{y}_i \sim f_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x_i)$ be a single sampled output

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N})$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} (s _ {i} - \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y} _ {i})) ^ {2}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote:
Recall that the response calibration Brier score (Equation (3)) is defined as:

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {r e s p o n s e}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} (s _ {i} - \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y} _ {i})) ^ {2}, \quad \hat {y} _ {i} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i}).
$$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $s _ {i} ^ {\mathrm {*, r e s p o n s e}}$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quantity: Expected correctness for input $x_i$ under model $f_\theta$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mu_ {i} \triangleq \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} [ \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y}) ]$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote: $$ \mu_ {i} \triangleq \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta} (\cdot | x _ {i})} [ \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y}) ], $$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {c a p a b i l i t y}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N})$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.definition: $\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {c a p a b i l i t y}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} (s _ {i} - \mu_ {i}) ^ {2}$
On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.quote: $$ \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {B r i e r}} ^ {\mathrm {c a p a b i l i t y}} (s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {N}) \triangleq \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} (s _ {i} - \mu_ {i}) ^ {2} = \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(s _ {i} - \mathbb {E} _ {\hat {y} \sim f _ {\theta (\cdot | x _ {i})}} [ \mathcal {C} (x _ {i}, \hat {y}) ]\right) ^ {2}. $$

On_the_Calibration_of_Large_Language_Mod.symbol: $s _ {i} ^ {\text {*, c a p a b i l i t y}}$

Privacy_Risk_in_Machine_Learning_Analyzi.definition: The membership experiment proceeds as follows: 1) Sample $S \sim \mathcal{D}^n$ , and let $A_S = A(S)$ . 2) Choose $b \leftarrow \{0,1\}$ uniformly at random. 3) Draw $z \sim S$ if $b = 0$ , or $z \sim \mathcal{D}$ if $b = 1$ 4) $\operatorname{Exp}^{\mathsf{M}}(\mathcal{A}, A, n, \mathcal{D})$ is 1 if $\mathcal{A}(z, A_S, n, \mathcal{D}) = b$ and 0 otherwise.
Privacy_Risk_in_Machine_Learning_Analyzi.quote:
Experiment 1 (Membership experiment $\mathsf{Exp}^{\mathsf{M}}(\mathcal{A}, A, n, \mathcal{D})$ ). Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an adversary, $A$ be a learning algorithm, $n$ be a positive integer, and $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution over data points $(x, y)$ . The membership experiment proceeds as follows:

1) Sample $S \sim \mathcal{D}^n$ , and let $A_S = A(S)$ .   
2) Choose $b \leftarrow \{0,1\}$ uniformly at random.   
3) Draw $z \sim S$ if $b = 0$ , or $z \sim \mathcal{D}$ if $b = 1$   
4) $\operatorname{Exp}^{\mathsf{M}}(\mathcal{A}, A, n, \mathcal{D})$ is 1 if $\mathcal{A}(z, A_S, n, \mathcal{D}) = b$ and 0 otherwise. $\mathcal{A}$ must output either 0 or 1.

We use $A = \text{prefix}(B)$ to represent that A is a prefix of B, indicating that $A = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{a})$ and $B = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{a}, \ldots, x_{a+b})$ for $b \geq 0$ .

By querying the language model with the root node $q$ times, we obtain $q$ token sets and their respective probabilities $p(X_{i:j}|X_{1:i-1}) = p(x_i|X_{1:i-1})p(x_{i+1}|X_{1:i})\ldots p(x_j|X_{1:j-1})$ .

Specifically, commencing from the root node and referencing the PUCT algorithm (Rosin, 2011), we select the next token set based on the formula:

$$
Y = \arg \max _ {X _ {i: j}} (v (X _ {i: j}; X _ {1: i - 1}) + c \cdot u (X _ {i: j}; X _ {1: i - 1})), \tag {1}

Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quote:
After we collect training data $\mathcal{D}_{\text{critic}}$ , we initialize $\mathcal{C}$ with a pre-trained LM and train it on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{critic}}$ using a standard conditional language modeling objective, maximizing likelihood:

$$
\max _ {\mathcal {C}} \mathbb {E} _ {((x, y), r) \sim \mathcal {D} _ {\text { critic }}} \log p _ {\mathcal {C}} (r | x, y), r \text {   for   reflection   tokens. } \tag {1}
$$

Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.definition: We train the generator model $\mathcal{M}$ by training on the curated corpus augmented with reflection tokens $\mathcal{D}_{gen}$ using the standard next token objective
Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quote:
We train the generator model $\mathcal{M}$ by training on the curated corpus augmented with reflection tokens $\mathcal{D}_{gen}$ using the standard next token objective:

$$
\max _ {\mathcal {M}} \mathbb {E} _ {(x, y, r) \sim \mathcal {D} _ {g e n}} \log p _ {\mathcal {M}} (y, r | x). \tag {2}
$$

Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quantity: Critic score, defined as the linear weighted sum of the normalized probability of each Critique token type
Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quote: $\mathcal {S} (\boxed {\text { Critique }}) = \sum_ {G \in \mathcal {G}} w ^ {G} s _ {t} ^ {G} \text {   for   } \mathcal {G} = \{\boxed {\text { ISREL }}, \boxed {\text { ISSUP }}, \boxed {\text { ISUSE }} \}, \tag {4}$

Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quantity: Score of critique token group $G$ at timestamp $t$, representing the generation probability of the most desirable reflection token
Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_a.quote: where $s_{t}^{G} = \frac{p_{t}(\hat{r})}{\sum_{i=1}^{NG} p_{t}(r_{i})}$ stands for the generation probability of the most desirable reflection token $\hat{r}$ (e.g., ISREL = Relevant) for the critique token type G with $N^{G}$ distinct tokens (that represent different possible values for G).

For ISREL, we compute the score as follows:

$$
s (\boxed {\mathrm{ISREL}}) = \frac {p (\boxed {\mathrm{ISREL}} = \text { RELEVANT })}{p (\boxed {\mathrm{ISREL}} = \text { RELEVANT }) + p (\boxed {\mathrm{ISREL}} = \text { IRRELEVANT })}.
$$

and compute the final scores as follows:

$$
s (\boxed {\mathrm{IsUSE}}) = \sum_ {i} ^ {5} w _ {i} \frac {p (\boxed {\mathrm{IsUSE}} = i)}{S},
$$

SHOW-O_ONE_SINGLE_TRANSFORMER_TO_UNIFY_M.definition: the forward process $q(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{x}_0) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} q(\mathbf{x}_t|\mathbf{x}_{t-1})$ corrupts the image data $x_0 \sim q(\mathbf{x}_0)$ into latent variables $x_1, \cdots, x_T$ in different noise level
SHOW-O_ONE_SINGLE_TRANSFORMER_TO_UNIFY_M.quote:
In diffusion models, the forward process $q(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{x}_0) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} q(\mathbf{x}_t|\mathbf{x}_{t-1})$ corrupts the image data $x_0 \sim q(\mathbf{x}_0)$ into latent variables $x_1, \cdots, x_T$ in different noise level.

$$ q(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{x}_0) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} q(\mathbf{x}_t|\mathbf{x}_{t-1}) $$

the transition distribution $q(\mathbf{x}_t|\mathbf{x}_{t-1})$ is commonly characterized by a Gaussian distribution:

$$
q (\mathbf {x} _ {t} | \mathbf {x} _ {t - 1}) = \mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} _ {t} | \sqrt {1 - \beta_ {t}} \mathbf {x} _ {t - 1}, \beta_ {t} \mathbf {I}), \tag {4},
$$

the transition distribution is instead formulated by a stochastic transition matrix $\mathbf{Q}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{(K+1) \times (K+1)}$ :

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{(K+1) \times (K+1)}
$$

where $[\mathbf{Q}_{t}]_{ij} = q(\mathbf{x}_{t} = j|\mathbf{x}_{t-1} = i)$

$$
[\mathbf{Q}_{t}]_{ij} = q(\mathbf{x}_{t} = j|\mathbf{x}_{t-1} = i)
$$

Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.quote:
Its PDF is given by:

$$
p _ {R L} (A; a) = \frac {A}{a ^ {2}} e ^ {\left(- \frac {A ^ {2}}{2 a ^ {2}}\right)}, \tag {1}
$$

Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.definition: $p _ {K} (A; v, \varphi , L) = \frac {2 \xi^ {(\beta + 1) / 2} A ^ {(\beta - 1) / 2}}{\Gamma (L) \Gamma (\varphi)} K _ {\varphi - L} \left(2 \sqrt {\xi A}\right)$
Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.quote:
Its PDF can be written as:

$$
p _ {K} (A; v, \varphi , L) = \frac {2 \xi^ {(\beta + 1) / 2} A ^ {(\beta - 1) / 2}}{\Gamma (L) \Gamma (\varphi)} K _ {\varphi - L} \left(2 \sqrt {\xi A}\right), \tag {2}
$$

Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.definition: $p _ {G} (A; a, d) = \frac {A ^ {d - 1} e ^ {- A / a}}{a ^ {d} \Gamma (d)} \text {f o r} a, d > 0$
Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.quote:
Its PDF belongs to a family of PDFs with two degrees of freedom, and is defined as (3):

$$
p _ {G} (A; a, d) = \frac {A ^ {d - 1} e ^ {- A / a}}{a ^ {d} \Gamma (d)} \text {f o r} a, d > 0, \tag {3}
$$

Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.definition: $p _ {G G} (A; a, d, p) = \frac {p A ^ {d - 1}}{a ^ {d} \Gamma (d / p)} e ^ {- (A / a) ^ {p}} \text {f o r} p > 0$
Signal-carrying_speckle_in_optical_coher.quote:
The Generalized Gamma (GG) distribution is a 3-parameter generalization of the Gamma distribution, with a PDF given by:

$$
p _ {G G} (A; a, d, p) = \frac {p A ^ {d - 1}}{a ^ {d} \Gamma (d / p)} e ^ {- (A / a) ^ {p}} \text {f o r} p > 0, \tag {4}
$$

The 2-parameter Weibull distribution [7], can be obtained from GG distribution for $d = p$ :

$$
